messages.subject: discrepant results accessing NBLAST via VFB site versus SI site
messages.subject_clean: discrepant results accessing NBLAST via VFB site versus SI site
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for this fantastic tool. We are now using NBLAST a lot to search and organize morphologies.
However, I've found discrepancies between the VFB and SI site.
Why are there discrepancies? Which version is more recent and/or more durable?

E.g., one cluster (here, "cluster 474") can look very different in the two sites:

http://flybrain.mrc-lmb.cam.ac.uk/si/nblast/clusters/clusters/474/webgl.html
http://flybrain.mrc-lmb.cam.ac.uk/vfb/fc/clusterv/3/fru-F-400114/

Another example: the same cluster can be named differently in the two sites:

http://flybrain.mrc-lmb.cam.ac.uk/si/nblast/clusters/clusters/637/
http://flybrain.mrc-lmb.cam.ac.uk/vfb/fc/clusterv/3/fru-F-700051/

messages.subject: Re: [nat-user] discrepant results accessing NBLAST via VFB site versus SI site
messages.subject_clean: [nat-user] discrepant results accessing NBLAST via VFB site versus SI site
messages.body_plain:
Dear Rachel,

Thanks for your interest. It’s great that you’re already finding the tools useful. Thanks also for writing to this list as you will probably not be the only person with these questions.

Indeed there are two separate sets of clusters and I agree this is not ideal. We decided to present only the central brain clusters in the SI (that is neurons with some arbours in the central brain, omitting those restricted to the optic lobe) because the results for the columnar regions of the optic lobe are not as good. However we had earlier released a full set of clusters to VFB and did not wish to remove those.

A few more specific comments inline.

On 19 Jul 2016, at 15:42, Rachel Wilson <rachel...@hms.harvard.edu> wrote:

> Thanks for this fantastic tool. We are now using NBLAST a lot to search and organize morphologies.
> However, I've found discrepancies between the VFB and SI site.
> Why are there discrepancies? Which version is more recent and/or more durable?
>
> E.g., one cluster (here, "cluster 474") can look very different in the two sites:
>
> http://flybrain.mrc-lmb.cam.ac.uk/si/nblast/clusters/clusters/474/webgl.html
> http://flybrain.mrc-lmb.cam.ac.uk/vfb/fc/clusterv/3/fru-F-400114/

These are not the same cluster. SI cluster 474 maps onto this cluster linked from VFB

http://flybrain.mrc-lmb.cam.ac.uk/vfb/fc/clusterv/3/fru-F-700092/

The recipe is to take the exemplar of the SI cluster (the one with score 1.0 e.g. fru-F-700092 <http://flybrain.mrc-lmb.cam.ac.uk/vfb/fc/clusterv/3/fru-F-700092/> ) and then append that to the base url

http://flybrain.mrc-lmb.cam.ac.uk/vfb/fc/clusterv/3/

> Another example: the same cluster can be named differently in the two sites:
>
> http://flybrain.mrc-lmb.cam.ac.uk/si/nblast/clusters/clusters/637/
> http://flybrain.mrc-lmb.cam.ac.uk/vfb/fc/clusterv/3/fru-F-700051/

Indeed.

Both clusters are durable in the sense that the URLs will continue to resolve even when we update the clusters that are returned by searching VFB.

@Marta, would you like to add anything.

Best,

Greg.

--
Gregory Jefferis, PhD
Division of Neurobiology
MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology
Francis Crick Avenue
Cambridge Biomedical Campus
Cambridge, CB2 OQH, UK

http://www2.mrc-lmb.cam.ac.uk/group-leaders/h-to-m/g-jefferis
http://jefferislab.org
http://flybrain.stanford.edu

messages.body_plain:
Hi Rachel,

It's great to know you find NBLAST useful.
The clusters on VFB include all of the FlyCircuit neurons, whereas the SI ones exclude the intrinsic optic lobe ones. So the cluster number and exemplar might be different between the sites. Though cluster composition itself might not differ that much.
We'll look into making that more explicit on both VFB and SI site. And I'll see if, for individual neuron pages on VFB like this (http://www.virtualflybrain.org/site/stacks/index.htm?id=VFB_00014678) we can add which cluster the neuron belongs to in the info section. That way you could search directly with a neuron identifier and check the cluster.

Best wishes,
Marta Costa

messages.subject: Re: problems with reformatting a swc
messages.body_plain:
Hi Greg,

I have been able to use the xform function to align swc files of traced neurons from different fish onto our standard brain. It works great so far but we occasionally see neurons in which the overall alignment worked well but individual points are a bit "jagged" which gives the neuron a bit of a "zig-zag" appearance. I attached a few examples. I assume the underlying problem is the initial alignment. Is there a specific parameter I need to tweak in order to prevent this from happening? Like something that tell CMTK not to move neighboring points to far away from each other?

Thanks,
Michael

messages.subject_clean: [nat-user] Re: problems with reformatting a swc
messages.body_plain:
Hi Michael,

This is almost certainly because some of these points cannot be transformed using the warping registration. By default they will be transformed using the affine component alone when the warp fails. However this can result in discontinuities. You can look at the help for xformpoints (called by xform) and it should give you details about the argument that controls this behaviour. If you turn it off you should start getting NAs for these points.

Looking at the images I cannot tell if these points are right on the surface of your template brain. It is very important that the template for registration includes all of the brain volume that you need since the warping transformation is undefined outside this region.

I do have some residual concerns that there might be a scale mismatch somewhere in your pipeline because I am surprised that you have undefined points. Were the sample image data used for registration and the sample data for tracing identical? If not are you 100% confident that you have corrected any space mismatches?

Best,

Greg.

Sent from my iPhone

messages.body_plain:
Ok. This is all a bit strange. You should turn off the fall back to affine option and see if the affected points become NAs. Assuming they do, it might be worth sharing the original image data (tracing image, un transformed tracing, registration image, template image, registration folder) off list. If the bad points are away from the surface my only other hypothesis is that there is a folding in the warping field in the low intensity part of your template - I have not seen that before. If that turns out to be the case there are registration parameters that can discourage that - possibly at the expense of some extra computation.

Best,

Greg.

Sent from my iPhone
